content:
Hi folks,

I'm exited to share early access for Axiom. We just released a free AI toolkit (CLI, Lean library, and AI skills) that makes it easy to translate regular ideas into formal ontology in Lean 4. This is very different from what most people are doing in Lean, but my dream is to see the rigor and epistemic humility of the math community expand to all domains of discourse. Critical feedback is appreciated!
Hi, can't seem to be able to access this/sign up for early access, is this still available?

Valentin Erokhin said:

Hi, can't seem to be able to access this/sign up for early access, is this still available?

Hi Valentin. It should still be available. Happy to help troubleshoot here or via DM. What is not working for you?
@Sam Cymbaluk trying to open https://axiomreason.com/ and it just redirects to https://coherencelabs.net/ , same happens when i press "Join early access" on that website

@Valentin Erokhin Ah, there was a stray AAAA record still redirecting :sweat_smile: I fixed it and purged DNS cache, but your machine might still have the bad record cached. Thanks for the bug report!
Anyone else thought this was about Axiom Math? This name is kinda confusing.

Is there some sort of whitepaper or design rationale? I've seen some amount of work in the AI sphere on formalizing natural language outputs from LLMs to find contradictions in the LLM output, generally using some existing linguistic frameworks. I feel like this is very similar in the mechanism, but seems to deviate a lot from those works.

In particular, looking at some examples, it doesn't look sufficiently "rigorous." A lot of the theorems are things I would expect to be heavily justified in natural language but instead bottoms out in opqaue semantic strings.

The graph design is pretty cool and I would love to see more projects adopt such a design.

I don't see the point of using Lean here. You don't need dependent types for everyday argumentation. And having the LLM "formalise" the user's beliefs (who presumably does not understand Lean) is nonsense.

Evan Wang said:

Is there some sort of whitepaper or design rationale?

We don't have a paper out yet, but that is a near term goal. Happy to answer any questions, or you can point your AI agent at the axiom-client repo which contains a lot of documentation. Philosophically, the project roughly aligns with Popper's critical rationalism and Wittgenstein's action-based semantics. We make heavy use of BFO (bfo-to-lean) and formal ontology best practices in general.

In particular, looking at some examples, it doesn't look sufficiently "rigorous." A lot of the theorems are things I would expect to be heavily justified in natural language but instead bottoms out in opqaue semantic strings.

That's exactly right. That mechanism is a key part of our approach. The idea is that instead of having to be extremely rigorous up front, you can state your beliefs with minimal formal structure and then iteratively refine the portions of an argument that are most criticized or questioned.

Jeremy Chen said:

I don't see the point of using Lean here. You don't need dependent types for everyday argumentation.

You're right. In practice, a lot of formal ontology is restricted to FOL. However, the goal with Axiom is to have a formal system for discourse that you "never need to leave". I believe dependent types are critical for that.

And having the LLM "formalise" the user's beliefs (who presumably does not understand Lean) is nonsense.

A few years ago, people thought it nonsense that AI would one day create software from the ideas of people who don't understand programming. Certainty there are challenges, but our semantic string approach handles a lot of the obvious ones quite well. The toolkit is completely free, if you do want to try.
